description_full: Align Technology, Inc. provides Invisalign clear aligners, Vivera retainers, and iTero intraoral scanners and services in the United States, Switzerland, and internationally. The company's Clear Aligner segment offers Invisalign comprehensive package to treat adults and teens malocclusion and features, and orthodontic needs of teenage or younger patients; and Invisalign First Phase I and Invisalign First Comprehensive Phase 2 package for younger patients between the ages of six and ten years with a mixture of primary/baby and permanent teeth. This segment also provides Invisalign express, Invisalign lite, and Invisalign moderate; Invisalign Go, Invisalign Go express, and Invisalign Go Plus; retention products, Invisalign training, adjusting tools used by dental professionals during treatment, ancillary Invisalign accessory products, and other oral health products; Invisalign Professional Whitening system; Invisalign Palatal Expander, a 3D printed orthodontic device; and 3D printing solutions. Its Imaging Systems and CAD/CAM Services segment offers iTero intraoral scanning system, a single hardware platform for restorative or orthodontic procedures; exocad, a computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacturing software; orthodontist software for digital records storage, orthodontic diagnosis, and fabrication of printed models and retainers; and restorative software for general practitioner dentists, prosthodontists, periodontists, and oral surgeons. This segment also offers Invisalign outcome simulator, a chair-side and cloud-based application for the iTero scanner; Invisalign progress assessment tool; Align Oral Health Suite, a digital interface for dental consultations; iTero TimeLapse technology for doctors or practitioners to compare a patient's historic 3D scans to the present-day scan; and subscription software, disposables, rents scanners, and pay per scan services. Align Technology, Inc. was incorporated in 1997 and is headquartered in Tempe, Arizona.

financial_summary: Align Technology, Inc. is a large-cap healthcare business with a $11.7B market cap on $4.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +17% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 15% against a 12% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 74% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $491M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.45× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.2% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 14% operating margin runs 13pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.54x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 458 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 6% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 1.42, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.84 vs 5y 1.65), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $137.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 54% in the 2020 crash, 73% in the 2022 bear market and 70% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 2% below its DCF fair value of $170, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 49%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $103 to $291 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Healthcare peers: EV/EBITDA 10.6 vs 15.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 33% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $186 on average, 12% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 11.8%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.64).
It runs a 74% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow, or 8% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.45x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 9.2% of revenue on R&D and 4.6% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $1.1B (9% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.8, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 129 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.6% over 3 years, 10.3% over 5 years and 16.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 28% of profits supports about 4.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -0.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.98, a backlog worth 34% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 6%.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (2.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 6.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (3.8% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 2.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 20,180 employees, each generates about $200K of revenue, 0.5x the Healthcare median, and productivity has risen 16.9% a year.
That works out to $24K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (13x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
